toc.title: Notifications and Alerts: SNS and SQS (skill 1.3.4)

html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. SNS: Simple Notification Service; SQS: Simple Queue Service; SDK: software development kit; VPC: Virtual Private Cloud; EMR: Elastic MapReduce; ETL: extract, transform, load; EC2: Elastic Compute Cloud; EKS: Elastic Kubernetes Service; ECS: Elastic Container Service; AI: artificial intelligence; KMS: Key Management Service; IAM: Identity and Access Management; MSK: Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka; AZ: Availability Zone; DMS: Database Migration Service; SAM: Serverless Application Model; CDK: Cloud Development Kit; SMS: Short Message Service; FIFO: first in, first out

  • Choose an orchestration service: Step Functions, Amazon MWAA (Apache Airflow), AWS Glue workflows, EventBridge, Lambda
  • Build pipelines for performance, availability, scalability, resiliency and fault tolerance
  • Implement and maintain serverless workflows
  • Send alerts with Amazon SNS and Amazon SQS

2What Orchestration Does

Running case

Kestrel Freight Chains Its Steps

  • Every night: load orders, clean them, join with telemetry, refresh the warehouse, then notify the team
  • A step sometimes fails because the source is slow
  • Finance wants a human approval before invoices are published
  • Your job: run the steps in order, with retries, branches and alerts
  • Orchestration coordinates many steps (jobs, queries, functions, approvals) into one workflow: order, dependencies, branching, parallel work, retries, error handling, state and monitoring
  • Choreography (events between loosely coupled services) is the alternative: no central coordinator; use EventBridge and SNS/SQS for it
  • A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a workflow with no loops: tasks and their dependencies

Service Pick it when Remember
AWS Step Functions Serverless, multi-service workflow with retries, branches, parallel and human approval State machine in JSON (Amazon States Language) with a visual editor; Standard and Express; 200+ services through the AWS SDK; pay per transition or execution
Amazon MWAA You already use Apache Airflow, need Python-coded DAGs, hundreds of operators and community plugins Managed Airflow: DAGs, requirements and plugins live in an S3 bucket; autoscaling workers; runs in your VPC; always-on environment cost
AWS Glue workflows A chain made only of Glue jobs and crawlers Triggers link jobs and crawlers; a start trigger (schedule, on demand or EventBridge event); run properties share state; visual graph
Amazon EventBridge Route events and schedule things; start other orchestrators Event bus (many-to-many), Pipes (point-to-point with filter and enrichment), Scheduler
AWS Lambda A single small step or glue code Do not build long workflows by chaining functions: no state, retries or visibility
Exam tip

"Serverless orchestration across Glue, Athena, Lambda and EMR with retry and error handling" → Step Functions. "Migrate existing Airflow DAGs" → Amazon MWAA.

3AWS Step Functions

Workflow types [Verify live]

Standard Express
Maximum duration One year Five minutes
Execution model Exactly once At least once (asynchronous Express)
Use for Long-running, auditable ETL and human approvals High-volume, short event processing
Service patterns Request response, .sync, callback Request response only
Billing Per state transition Per execution, duration and memory
History In Step Functions (kept 90 days) CloudWatch Logs only

Service integration patterns

  • Request Response: call a service and go on at once after the HTTP response
  • Run a Job (.sync): call a service and wait until the job finishes: AWS Glue, Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR (on EC2, on EKS, Serverless), AWS Batch, Amazon ECS/Fargate, Amazon EKS, AWS Glue DataBrew, SageMaker AI, CodeBuild, Bedrock and nested Step Functions
  • Wait for Callback (.waitForTaskToken): pass a task token and pause (up to the one-year limit) until a worker calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure: used for human approval and external systems; add a HeartbeatSeconds timeout so a lost token does not hang the run
  • Optimized integrations (Glue, Athena, EMR, Batch, SNS, SQS, Lambda, DynamoDB and more) and AWS SDK integrations (over 200 services)

Flow control and error handling

  • State types: Task, Choice (branch), Parallel, Map (loop over items, including Distributed Map for very large item sets in Standard workflows), Wait, Pass, Succeed, Fail
  • Retry (error names, interval, max attempts, backoff rate, jitter) and Catch (route failures to a fallback state, such as an SNS alert)
  • Timeouts (TimeoutSeconds) and heartbeats stop stuck tasks
Exam tip

"Wait for a Glue job to finish before the next step" → the .sync integration (glue:startJobRun.sync). "Pause until a manager approves" → .waitForTaskToken.

4Amazon MWAA (Managed Apache Airflow)

  • Apache Airflow is open-source software to author, schedule and monitor workflows as Python code (DAGs)
  • Amazon MWAA runs it without servers to manage: AWS sets up and patches Airflow, scales workers automatically between a minimum and maximum, runs the scheduler and workers in its own VPC and encrypts with KMS
  • Deploy: put DAG files (and requirements.txt, plugins) in an S3 bucket; the environment picks them up
  • Access: the Airflow web UI is public or private (VPC endpoint); permissions come from IAM; operators call Glue, EMR, Athena, Redshift, Batch, Lambda, SageMaker AI, SQS, SNS and S3
  • Monitoring: Airflow task and scheduler logs and metrics go to CloudWatch
  • Scheduling is part of the DAG (schedule interval or cron), so MWAA also covers skill 1.1.5
  • Trade-off: more powerful and portable, but you pay for the environment while it exists and write Python
Step Functions Amazon MWAA
Model State machine (JSON), visual Python DAGs
Operations Fully serverless, pay per use Managed environment, always running
Best for AWS-native workflows, event-driven, human approval Existing Airflow, rich operators, complex scheduling and backfills
Exam tip

MWAA troubleshooting starts in CloudWatch Logs (scheduler, worker, DAG processing) and the DAGs in S3 (Module 10).

5AWS Glue Workflows and EventBridge

Glue workflows

  • A workflow orchestrates crawlers, jobs and triggers and records the status of each step as a graph
  • A start trigger is a schedule (cron), on demand, or an EventBridge event (for example an object arriving in S3), optionally batched by event count and a window (default and maximum 900 seconds)
  • Triggers inside the workflow fire when previous jobs or crawlers succeed, fail or time out
  • Run properties are name/value pairs shared between jobs in a run
  • Keep a workflow to 100 or fewer jobs, crawlers and triggers
  • Use blueprints to create common workflows

Amazon EventBridge

  • Event bus: many-to-many routing with rules and event patterns; sources include AWS services, SaaS partners and your apps
  • Pipes: point-to-point from a source (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, MSK and more) through optional filter and enrichment to a target (such as Step Functions); you pay only for events that match the filter
  • Scheduler: time-based starts (Module 1)
  • Glue job state changes and many other service events appear on EventBridge, so a rule can send a failure alert or start the next pipeline
Exam tip

"A new file in S3 must start a multi-step pipeline" → S3 → EventBridge rule → Step Functions (or a Glue workflow).

6Building Reliable, Scalable Pipelines (skill 1.3.2)

Quality Design choices
Performance Parallel branches and Map iterations; right-sized engines; columnar data; avoid serial steps that could run together
Scalability Serverless and auto scaling services (Glue, Lambda, Step Functions, on-demand Kinesis); decouple stages with queues and streams
Availability Managed multi-AZ services; no single server; multi-AZ MWAA and DMS; cross-Region copies for disaster recovery
Resiliency and fault tolerance Retries with backoff, dead-letter queues, checkpoints and bookmarks, idempotent steps, timeouts, catch and compensate, partial reruns from the failed step
Operability Logs, metrics, alarms, correlation IDs, tags; infrastructure as code for repeatable deployments
  • Idempotent means a step can run twice with the same result (overwrite a partition, upsert by key): the basis of safe retries
  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ): a queue that keeps messages that could not be processed after a set number of tries, for inspection and redrive
  • Decoupling with SQS: producers write to a queue; consumers scale on queue depth and absorb bursts
Exam tip

"A downstream service is slow or fails sometimes and the pipeline must not lose data" → put an SQS queue (with a DLQ) between the stages and make the consumer idempotent.

7Serverless Workflows (skill 1.3.3)

  • A serverless workflow uses managed, auto-scaling services and no servers to patch: Step Functions (control), Lambda and Glue (compute), EventBridge (events and schedules), SQS and SNS (messaging), S3, DynamoDB, Athena (data)
  • Implement: define the state machine, grant least-privilege IAM roles per step, set retries, timeouts and catches, add alarms, deploy with IaC (AWS SAM, CloudFormation, CDK: Module 5)
  • Maintain: version and alias Lambda functions; version state machines; watch CloudWatch metrics and logs; review failed executions; keep costs in check (Express for high volume, Standard for long runs)
  • AWS Glue and Athena are serverless; MWAA and EMR on EC2 are not

8Notifications and Alerts: SNS and SQS (skill 1.3.4)

Amazon SNS Amazon SQS
Model Publish/subscribe (push) Queue (pull)
Delivery One message → many subscribers: email, SMS, mobile push, HTTP, Lambda, SQS, Firehose One message → one consumer at a time
Use for Alerts, fan-out Buffering, decoupling, work queues
Features Message filtering by attributes; FIFO topics Standard (at least once, best-effort order) and FIFO (exactly once, ordered); DLQ; visibility timeout; long polling; retention up to 14 days
  • Alert pattern: CloudWatch alarm or EventBridge rule (for example a failed Glue job) → SNS topic → email, chat bot, ticketing or Lambda
  • Fan-out pattern: SNS topic → several SQS queues, each feeding a different consumer
  • Step Functions can publish to SNS or send to SQS directly (Catch states often do)
Exam tip

"Notify the team when a pipeline fails" → EventBridge or CloudWatch alarm → SNS. "Buffer records so consumers can process at their own pace" → SQS.

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Kestrel Freight's nightly pipeline must run an AWS Glue job, wait for it to finish, run an Athena query, and send a notification if any step fails. The team wants no servers to manage. Which service should orchestrate it?

  • AAmazon MWAA with a custom Airflow environment
  • BA cron job on an EC2 instance
  • CAWS Lambda calling the next Lambda function
  • DAWS Step Functions
Show the answer

Answer: D. Step Functions is serverless, integrates with Glue and Athena with the Run a Job pattern, and supports retries and catch states. MWAA is not serverless, and chained Lambda functions lack state and visibility.

S2A company already has hundreds of Apache Airflow DAGs written in Python. It wants to move them to AWS with the least change. Which service fits?

  • AAWS Step Functions Express workflows with Choice and Map states
  • BAWS Glue workflows with scheduled and conditional triggers only
  • CAmazon EventBridge Pipes with an SQS queue as the source
  • DAmazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow
Show the answer

Answer: D. Amazon MWAA runs Apache Airflow, so existing DAGs, operators and plugins can be reused, with DAGs stored in S3.

S3A Step Functions workflow must pause until a manager approves an invoice outside AWS, then continue. Which integration pattern should be used?

  • ARequest Response, which continues after the HTTP response
  • BWait for a Callback with Task Token, using SendTaskSuccess
  • CRun a Job (.sync), which waits for an AWS service job to end
  • DA Choice state that compares the invoice amount with a limit
Show the answer

Answer: B. The callback pattern pauses the task until an external process returns the task token with SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure; add a heartbeat timeout so a lost token does not hang the run.

S4A step in a data pipeline sometimes fails because the downstream service is briefly overloaded. The pipeline must not lose records and must tolerate the slow service. Which TWO design choices help? (Select TWO.)

  • ADisable timeouts
  • BRun all steps in one very large Lambda function
  • CAdd an Amazon SQS queue with a dead-letter queue between the stages
  • DMake the consumer step idempotent so retries do not create duplicates
  • ERemove all retries so failures are visible immediately
Show the answer

Answer: C, D. A queue decouples the stages and absorbs slowness, a dead-letter queue keeps messages that keep failing, and idempotent consumers make retries safe. The other options remove safeguards.

S5A pipeline made only of AWS Glue jobs and crawlers must start when a new object arrives in S3 and show the status of each step as a graph. What is the simplest option?

  • AAn AWS Glue workflow with an EventBridge event start trigger
  • BAmazon MWAA with an S3 sensor in a long DAG schedule
  • CA long-running Amazon EMR cluster that polls the bucket each minute
  • DAn Amazon SQS FIFO queue with a consumer on EC2 instances
Show the answer

Answer: A. Glue workflows orchestrate jobs and crawlers, can be started by an EventBridge event such as an S3 object arriving, and display the run as a graph.

S6Which statement about Step Functions Express workflows is correct?

  • AThey can run for up to one year and keep exactly-once execution for every state
  • BThey suit high-volume, short event processing and run for up to five minutes
  • CThey support the Run a Job (.sync) and callback integration patterns
  • DThey keep the full execution history inside Step Functions for 90 days
Show the answer

Answer: B. Express workflows run up to five minutes, are built for high-volume short workloads, support only the Request Response pattern, and send history to CloudWatch Logs.
